messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tama, a 71-year-old painter who lived alone in a small coastal town in California, had spent most of his life working on large-scale murals and fine art commissions, his reputation built on steady hands and a calm presence. That changed one afternoon three years ago, when he was waiting for a bus near a crowded market. A bomb hidden in a trash can detonated fifty feet away. The blast threw him to the ground. He remembered the pressure in his chest, the ringing in his ears, and the sight of a woman's shoe lying beside his face, still laced. He had not been physically injured, but something in him had shifted that day and never settled back.

In the weeks after, Tama found that the memory of the explosion would force its way into his mind without warning. He would be mixing paint on his palette, and suddenly he would feel his body tense as though he were again lying on the pavement, his arms pinned beneath him, his cheek pressed against the cold concrete. The memory was not just visual; it was bodily. He could feel the exact angle of his neck and the grit against his skin, and the clarity of those sensations terrified him. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, and that he could not rely on other people to keep him safe. He also began to feel that he could not rely on himself, because his own mind kept pulling him back into that moment without his permission, and he could not stop it.

To manage this, Tama tried hard to control his emotions. When he felt the familiar tightness in his chest or the surge of fear, he would clench his jaw and force himself to focus on something neutral—the grain of a wooden floorboard, the pattern of light on the wall. He also began asking his neighbor, a younger man named Leo, to check in on him each evening. Tama would call Leo and say, "I'm fine, right? Everything is okay?" and Leo would reassure him that he was safe and that nothing bad was happening. This helped for a few minutes, but then the memory would return, and Tama would feel the need to call again. The more he sought reassurance, the more the memories intruded, and the more convinced he became that he could not manage on his own.

He stopped going out. He had always worked from a studio attached to his house, so the practical impact was not immediate, but over months it became severe. He stopped buying fresh paint supplies. He stopped walking to the corner store for coffee. He told himself that the world outside was unpredictable, that he could not control what might happen. What frightened him most was the thought that his own reactions would fail him—that if something unexpected occurred, he would freeze or fall apart, and that no one would be there to help. This belief reinforced his need to control his emotions and to ask for reassurance, which in turn made the memories more frequent and more vivid. He noticed that after he called Leo, the memory would surface again within an hour, sometimes with even more detail.

The cycle tightened over two years. Tama's painting slowed, then stopped. He had not completed a commission in over a year, and his savings were running low. Leo had begun to sound tired on the phone, and Tama was certain that he was annoying him, but he could not stop calling. He was afraid that if he stopped seeking reassurance, the fear would become unbearable and he would have no way to manage it. He was also afraid that if he let himself feel the emotions fully, he would not be able to stop them.

What finally brought Tama to seek help was a morning when he could not bring himself to open his front door to collect the mail. He stood in the hallway for twenty minutes, his hand on the lock, his heart pounding, his body remembering the concrete and the blast. He called his doctor that afternoon. He was hoping that someone could tell him how to make the memories stop, and he was afraid that nothing would work.
